summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

primary_citations.citation_text: District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 4-1321.07 (Failure to make report)
District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 16-2304 (Right to counsel; party status)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: A plaintiff suing the District for negligent placement and monitoring of a foster child who died must present expert testimony on the applicable standard of care, and the foster mother was not the District's agent for respondeat superior purposes.
key_cases.relevance: It is the practical barrier, expert testimony on the standard of care, that defeats most D.C. claims arising from a death in foster care.
key_cases.quote: Mrs. Hampton should have presented expert testimony on the standard of care, and that the absence of such testimony was fatal to her case

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
key_cases.holding: A youth in the District's legal custody and placed by it in a group program was in state custody for DeShaney purposes, so the District owed him a substantive due process duty of care and the jury's deliberate-indifference verdict was sustained.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading D.C. Circuit case imposing § 1983 liability on the District for deliberate indifference in selecting and monitoring a placement provider.
key_cases.quote: Because the District, rather than Tron's family, had primary legal control over him, the District had legal responsibility for his daily care.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: When CPS receives a report identifying particular children as abused, the Child Abuse Prevention Act creates a special relationship imposing on the District a duty to take the steps the Act prescribes for those children, so summary judgment for the District was error.
key_cases.relevance: It is the leading D.C. special-relationship case for holding the District liable after harm to children it was told about.
key_cases.quote: From that moment on, the District had a duty to take certain steps prescribed by the Act for the protection of those children.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, so caseworkers who left Joshua in his abusive father's custody were not liable under § 1983; a duty arises only where the State takes the person into its own custody.
key_cases.relevance: It draws the custody line that determines whether a death under agency supervision is a constitutional violation or only a tort.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.case_name: Doe ex rel. Fein v. District of Columbia
key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Police reports of a child's injuries did not satisfy the six-month written notice requirement of D.C. Code § 12-309, and the statute does not permit equitable tolling, so the abused child's claims against the District and its employees were barred.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that § 12-309's six-month notice period is jurisdictional in effect and cannot be equitably tolled, even for an injured infant.
key_cases.quote: the police reports filed after Jane Doe suffered her physical injuries were insufficient under D.C.Code § 12-309 to provide the District with notice of her potential claims

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc the court affirmed the dismissal of negligence suits against the District for failure to provide adequate police services, holding that the duty to furnish public services is owed to the public at large and that no individual can sue for its breach absent a special relationship giving rise to a specific legal duty to that person.
key_cases.relevance: It is the general rule of municipal non-liability out of which Turner v. District of Columbia carves the narrow child-abuse-reporting exception, so a brief citing Turner without it makes the District look far more suable than it is.
key_cases.quote: The duty to provide public services is owed to the public at large, and, absent a special relationship between the police and an individual, no specific legal duty exists.
